summary_html: Agency or court authorizes **immediate medical or psychological care** when delay endangers life or safety. Federal statutes support medical access and confidentiality exceptions for child protection.

key_cases.case_name: Lowther v. Children, Youth & Families Department
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed qualified immunity for an investigator and county defendants on a warrantless-entry claim, holding that under circuit precedent a reasonable official could believe reasonable suspicion of past abuse justified warrantless entry, so the law was not clearly established to the contrary.
key_cases.relevance: Where officials enter to check on a child's medical or physical condition, the exigency analysis in this case governs the constitutionality of that entry.
key_cases.quote: a reasonable investigator or officer could reasonably believe warrantless entry was justified by reasonable suspicion of past abuse

key_cases.case_name: T.H. v. University of Kansas Hospital Authority
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of a malpractice suit against a physician who reported suspected sexual abuse, holding that K.S.A. 38-2223(f) immunizes reporters who negligently misdiagnose abuse and that the immunity is lost only if the plaintiff pleads facts supporting actual malice, meaning a specific intent to injure.
key_cases.relevance: Medical professionals who act on a suspicion of abuse in the course of emergency evaluation and examination are shielded from negligence liability for doing so.
key_cases.quote: In sum, we find that K.S.A. 2015 Supp. 38-2223(f) provides immunity to doctors who negligently misdiagnose child abuse
